tip: Hindi has no 'the' or 'a' – सब्ज़ी मंडी बंद है (sabzi mandi band hai) is just 'vegetable market closed is'. Context alone tells you which market.
होते हैं (hote hain) marks a general truth: ज़रूरी होते हैं (zaroori hote hain = are, as a rule, necessary). Plain हैं (hain) would pin it to right now.
English says 'has been raining'; Hindi keeps plain 'is raining': बारिश हो रही है (barish ho rahi hai = rain is happening) + सुबह से (subah se = since morning).
क्या (kya) up front is a spoken question mark: क्या यह सच है (kya yeh sach hai) = is this true? Without it, यह सच है (yeh sach hai) states 'this is true'.
Things 'come into' a space when they fit: ज़्यादा सामान नहीं आता (zyada saman nahin aata = more stuff doesn't come) = no more fits. Rooms, boxes, clothes all work this way.
-कर (-kar) glued to a verb means 'after doing it': उठकर (uthkar = having gotten up). One ending does the work of English 'after waking up'.
के लिए (ke liye = for) comes after its noun, not before: बुखार के लिए (bukhar ke liye = fever for). Hindi's little linking words all trail the noun.
मुझे ... करना है (mujhe ... karna hai) is literally 'to me it is to-do' – Hindi's 'I have to'. फ़ोन करना है (phone karna hai) = I have to make a call.
भी (bhi) normally means 'also', but next to नहीं (nahin) it means 'at all': बिलकुल भी अच्छा नहीं (bilkul bhi achha nahin) = not good at all.
The battery 'became finished': ख़त्म हो गई है (khatm ho gayi hai). Hindi frames new states as becoming – phones die, tanks fill, trains run late by 'becoming'.
You don't spend a childhood in Hindi – it passes on its own: बीता था (beeta tha = passed). बचपन (bachpan = childhood) is the subject; the village is just where it happened.
Liking lands on you: तुम्हें (tumhein = to you) plus अच्छा लगता है (achha lagta hai = strikes as good) = you like it. The person liking is the target, not the doer.
The plain present doubles as 'let's': कल बात करते हैं (kal baat karte hain = we talk tomorrow) actually offers 'let's talk tomorrow'. No extra word needed.
Superlatives are 'from all': सबसे तेज़ (sabse tez = fast beyond all) = fastest. No -est ending in Hindi – सबसे (sabse) before any adjective does it.
English can drop 'that' – 'I'm sure you can'. Hindi never drops कि: मुझे यक़ीन है कि (mujhe yaqeen hai ki = I'm sure that). The कि (ki) always stays.
वाला (wala) picks out a specific one: यह वाला (yeh wala) = this one. It works with colors, sizes, and prices in any shop.
चार बजे (char baje = at four) is literally 'four struck' – Hindi counts clock time in bell strikes, so there is no separate word for 'o'clock'.
दो (do = give) added to a verb aims the action at someone else: ठीक कर दो (theek kar do) = fix it for me. The 'give' points the favor toward the asker.
Hindi has no verb 'to have' – things sit near you: मेरे पास (mere paas = near me) + समय नहीं है (samay nahin hai = there's no time) = I don't have time.
